Fourier series (f(x)∼a0​/2+∑n≥1​[an​cos(nx)+bn​sin(nx)])

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Analysis
OurBigBook.com Words: 6k Articles: 98
A Fourier series describes a periodic function through sines and cosines whose frequencies are integer multiples of one base frequency. These Fourier harmonics give a useful alternative to describing the value at every input: each Fourier coefficient measures how much of one oscillating pattern is present. For a real, integrable function of period 2π, the real form is
f(x)∼2a0​​+∑n=1∞​[an​cos(nx)+bn​sin(nx)],an​=π1​∫−ππ​f(x)cos(nx)dx,bn​=π1​∫−ππ​f(x)sin(nx)dx.
(1)
The cosine formula includes n=0; the sine formula uses n≥1. Thus a0​/2 is the mean value over a period, not a0​ itself. The symbol ∼ associates a function with its Fourier coefficients; an equality requires a specified kind of convergence, such as pointwise convergence. For general period T>0, replace nx by 2πnt/T and the coefficient prefactor by 2/T. Fourier orthogonality explains why integrating against one mode removes the others. [ref].
For a finite example, take
f(x)=21​+cosx+21​sin(2x).
(2)
Its mean is 1/2, its real Fourier coefficients are a0​=1, a1​=1, b2​=1/2, and all other an​,bn​ vanish. At x=π/4, the three contributions add to 1/2+1/2​+1/2=1+1/2​≈1.70710678. The function is already a trigonometric polynomial, so retaining these modes reconstructs it exactly. Here x is an angular coordinate in radians; if it instead represents time, a base angular frequency must supply the corresponding units.
The change of viewpoint is useful because many linear problems act separately on these modes. The second derivative maps sin(nx) to −n2sin(nx) and maps cos(nx) in the same way. Consequently a differential equation that is complicated for a whole profile can become a simpler calculation for each Fourier harmonic. A linear time-invariant system similarly has a separate response to each complex exponential. Superposition combines the responses when the relevant sums and operations are justified. [ref].
The infinite case contains a subtlety absent from the finite example. Under pointwise convergence of a piecewise smooth Fourier series, the value at a jump discontinuity is the average of the two one-sided limits. For a square-integrable function, the complex Fourier series instead converges in the L2 norm: the integrated squared error tends to zero. Neither statement says that the error becomes small everywhere at once. A square wave shows the difference vividly through the Gibbs phenomenon.
A historical source for this connection between profiles and modes is Joseph Fourier's 1822 book Théorie analytique de la chaleur. Chapter III develops expansions in sines and cosines while studying the propagation of heat. The heat equation gives a continuing application of this approach. [ref].

Dini test for Fourier series (∫0δ​∣f(t+s)+f(t−s)−L+​−L−​∣ds/s<∞)

Words: 114
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
For an integrable periodic function with one-sided limits L+​,L−​ at t, the displayed condition implies that its classical Fourier partial sums converge to (L+​+L−​)/2. To prove it use the Dirichlet kernel Dn​(s)=sin((n+1/2)s)/sin(s/2) and its integral 2π. Subtract the target value and combine the positive and negative halves of the convolution integral. The resulting difference is
2π1​∫0π​sin(s/2)f(t+s)+f(t−s)−L+​−L−​​sin((n+1/2)s)ds.
(3)
The coefficient of the sine is integrable near zero by the Dini condition, and away from zero by integrability of f. The Riemann-Lebesgue lemma therefore makes this expression tend to zero. Step functions satisfy the condition because the numerator vanishes in a sufficiently small punctured neighborhood. This is a local Fourier convergence test, distinct from Dini's theorem on uniform convergence of monotone sequences of continuous functions.

Lacunary Fourier series (nj+1​/nj​≥q>1)

Words: 152 Articles: 1
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
A Hadamard-lacunary Fourier series has nonzero frequencies supported on a positive sequence with the displayed gap ratio, possibly together with its negatives and finitely many extra modes. Such gaps strongly restrict additive frequency relations. They make moment estimates resemble those of independent random variables. For a ratio greater than three, the strongly lacunary polynomial L1-L2 bound follows directly by enumerating fourth-moment pairings.

Strongly lacunary polynomial L1-L2 bound (∥p∥2​≤3​∥p∥1​)

Words: 97
Lacunary Fourier series OurBigBook.com
Use normalized measure on the circle. If a trigonometric polynomial has frequency support {±nj​} with nj+1​>3nj​, every zero sum of four signed frequencies pairs into opposite equal frequencies: the largest unpaired term would exceed the sum of the other three. Expanding the fourth moment and bounding its three possible pairings gives ∥p∥44​≤3∥p∥24​. The Holder inequality gives ∥p∥2​≤∥p∥11/3​∥p∥42/3​ and hence the displayed estimate. Therefore an L1 function with only these lacunary frequencies has square-summable coefficients: apply the estimate to its uniformly L1-bounded Fejér sums and then pass to finite coefficient blocks. Finitely many extra modes do not affect the conclusion.

Orthogonality of trigonometric functions (∫0L​sin(nπx/L)sin(mπx/L)dx=(L/2)δmn​)

Words: 90
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
For positive integers m,n, the sine functions form an orthogonal family on (0,L):
∫0L​sin(Lnπx​)sin(Lmπx​)dx=2L​δmn​.
(4)
The same formula holds for the corresponding cosine functions when both indices are positive. Product-to-sum identities reduce the distinct-index products to cosines with nonzero integer frequencies, each with zero integral; for matching indices, the squared sine or cosine has mean 1/2. This proves the formula and explains why separate normal modes of a uniform fixed-end string make additive contributions to its kinetic energy and potential energy. The constant cosine has squared norm L rather than L/2.

Dirichlet's theorem on Fourier series (SN​f(x)→[f(x−)+f(x+)]/2)

Words: 42
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
One standard sufficient form states that the Fourier series of a piecewise continuously differentiable periodic function converges at x to [f(x−)+f(x+)]/2. At a continuity point it equals f(x). This modern sufficient form should be distinguished from the exact hypotheses of the 1829 original.[ref]

Fourier series of a periodic rectangular pulse (an​=(2/T)sinc(πnw/T))

Words: 107 Articles: 1
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
An even train of rectangular pulses of width w<T, period T and unit area per pulse has Fourier coefficients an​=(2/T)sinc(πnw/T) for n≥0. Here the sinc function is normalized as sincz=sinz/z, and the constant contribution is a0​/2=1/T. Integrating the cosine over the pulse proves the formula; evenness eliminates the sine coefficients. At a pulse edge, pointwise convergence of a piecewise smooth Fourier series gives the mean of the one-sided values rather than a prescribed endpoint value.

Pulse-width scale of Fourier coefficients (n∼T/w)

Words: 43
Fourier series of a periodic rectangular pulse OurBigBook.com
For the Fourier series of a periodic rectangular pulse, the sinc function is nearly one when nw/T≪1 and has its first zero at nw/T=1. Thus narrowing a pulse increases the range of significant Fourier coefficients. Only integer harmonic indices occur, so an envelope zero need not be an exactly vanishing coefficient.

Fourier series of a half-wave rectified ramp (f(x)=x+∣x∣(−1<x<1))

Words: 83
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
Extend f(x)=max(0,2x) on (−1,1) with period two. Its Fourier coefficients in the basis cos(nπx),sin(nπx) are a0​=1, an​=2[(−1)n−1]/(nπ)2, and bn​=2(−1)n+1/(nπ), by integration by parts on (0,1). Thus
f(x)∼21​−π24​∑r=0∞​(2r+1)2cos((2r+1)πx)​+π2​∑n=1∞​n(−1)n+1sin(nπx)​.
(5)
Its even part is the periodic extension of ∣x∣ and its odd part is the Fourier series of a periodic sawtooth for x. The cosine terms converge absolutely and uniformly; the sine terms account for the jump at odd integers. At each jump, the full Fourier series has value 1, the average of the two one-sided limits 0 and 2.

Fourier series of a noninteger-frequency cosine (cos(μx),μ∈R∖Z)

Words: 91
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
Extend cos(μx) from [−π,π] with period 2π. It is an even function, so all sine Fourier coefficients vanish. The product-to-sum identity gives
a0​=πμ2sin(πμ)​,an​=π(μ2−n2)2μ(−1)nsin(πμ)​(n≥1).
(6)
Indeed, integrate cos(μx)cos(nx) on [0,π] and use sin(π(μ±n))=(−1)nsin(πμ). Thus
f(x)=πμsin(πμ)​+π2μsin(πμ)​∑n=1∞​μ2−n2(−1)ncos(nx)​.
(7)
The coefficients are O(n−2), so the series converges absolutely and uniformly. The Dirichlet-Jordan convergence theorem identifies it with the periodic function everywhere, including the endpoints because the two endpoint values agree. Substituting a noninteger rational frequency and a convenient x yields explicit series sums. Integer frequencies require taking removable limits rather than substituting into a zero denominator.

Fourier solution of a first-order equation with periodic forcing (αy′+βy=f)

Words: 104
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
Let α,β be nonzero real constants and let f be a smooth periodic function of period 2π, with real Fourier coefficients cn​,dn​. Write the unknown periodic solution with Fourier coefficients an​,bn​. Fourier orthogonality applied to the equation gives
βa0​=c0​,βan​+αnbn​=cn​,βbn​−αnan​=dn​.
(8)
Solving these two-by-two linear systems gives
an​=β2+α2n2βcn​−αndn​​,bn​=β2+α2n2αncn​+βdn​​(n≥1).
(9)
The smooth forcing has rapidly decreasing Fourier coefficients, so the resulting series and its derivatives converge and satisfy the equation. Uniqueness follows because the difference of two solutions is Ce−βx/α, which is periodic only when C=0. A single sinusoidal forcing therefore gives a single sinusoidal response with changed amplitude and phase.

Fourier series of a periodically extended exponential (f(x)=eκx,−L<x<L)

Words: 80
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
Let L>0 and real κ=0. Extend eκx with period 2L. In the Fourier series convention a0​/2+∑n≥1​[an​cos(nπx/L)+bn​sin(nπx/L)], put qn​=nπ/L. Direct integration gives
a0​=κL2sinh(κL)​,an​=L(κ2+qn2​)2κ(−1)nsinh(κL)​,bn​=−L(κ2+qn2​)2qn​(−1)nsinh(κL)​.
(10)
For example, the required antiderivatives are eκx(κcosqn​x+qn​sinqn​x)/(κ2+qn2​) and eκx(κsinqn​x−qn​cosqn​x)/(κ2+qn2​). The Dirichlet-Jordan convergence theorem gives the exponential value away from the jumps and their midpoint cosh(κL) at odd multiples of L. For κ=0, the function is identically one, with a0​=2 and all other Fourier coefficients zero.

Fourier series of a half-wave rectified sinusoid

Words: 68
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
For V(t)=V0​max(sinωt,0), with period 2π/ω, half-wave rectification gives
V(t)=πV0​​+2V0​​sinωt−π2V0​​∑m=1∞​4m2−1cos(2mωt)​.
(11)
The Fourier coefficients are a0​=2V0​/π, b1​=V0​/2, a2m​=−2V0​/[π(4m2−1)], with all remaining coefficients zero. To derive the cosine coefficients, integrate sinscosns over 0<s<π and use the product-to-sum identity. The sine coefficients follow from orthogonality. A half-period delay reverses only the fundamental sine term and leaves the constant and even-frequency cosine terms unchanged, by translation of a Fourier series.

Translation of a Fourier series

Words: 59
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
For a period-L Fourier series written as a0​/2+∑n≥1​(an​coskn​x+bn​sinkn​x), where kn​=2πn/L, translating the function by ℓ to g(x)=f(x−ℓ) rotates each pair of Fourier coefficients:
an(g)​=an​cos(kn​ℓ)−bn​sin(kn​ℓ),bn(g)​=an​sin(kn​ℓ)+bn​cos(kn​ℓ).
(12)
The constant coefficient is unchanged. These formulas follow by the sine and cosine subtraction identities. In the complex Fourier series, the same statement is g​n​=e−ikn​ℓf​n​. An integer-period translation changes no Fourier coefficient.

Fourier series of periodic hyperbolic sine and cosine

Words: 124
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
For β>0, periodically extend cosh(βx) and sinh(βx) from −1<x≤1 with period 2. Their Fourier series are
cosh(βx)=βsinhβ​+2βsinhβ∑n=1∞​β2+n2π2(−1)ncos(nπx)​,
(13)
and, away from odd integers,
sinh(βx)=2πsinhβ∑n=1∞​β2+n2π2(−1)n+1nsin(nπx)​.
(14)
The first identity follows by integration of cosh(βx)cos(nπx) on [−1,1], using the antiderivative
β2+n2π2βsinh(βx)cos(nπx)+nπcosh(βx)sin(nπx)​.
(15)
For the second identity, integration by parts and dcosh(βx)/dx=βsinh(βx) show that its sine coefficient is −nπ/β times the first series' cosine coefficient. This avoids assuming that a Fourier series can always be differentiated term by term. The periodic hyperbolic cosine is continuous, so its series converges to it everywhere. The periodic hyperbolic sine has a jump discontinuity at each odd integer: the Dirichlet-Jordan convergence theorem gives the average of its two limiting values, namely zero, there. Both identities hold in the sense of mean-square convergence, which suffices for Parseval's identity.

Square wave (sgn(sinθ)=π4​∑n≥1, n odd​nsinnθ​)

Words: 200 Articles: 1
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
A square wave alternates between two constant levels for equal halves of a period. Choose a 2π-periodic function equal to 1 on (0,π) and −1 on (−π,0), with value zero at the jumps. Its odd function symmetry makes the mean and every cosine Fourier coefficient vanish. Directly integrating the two constant pieces gives
a0​=an​=0,bn​=πn2[1−(−1)n]​,f(x)∼π4​∑k=0∞​2k+1sin((2k+1)x)​.
(16)
Thus only odd sine Fourier harmonics occur, with amplitudes decreasing like the reciprocal of their frequency multiplier. Every finite Fourier partial sum is smooth, yet their pointwise limit has jumps. At those jumps the Fourier series converges to zero, the midpoint of the two levels, regardless of which value we assign to the original function there.
This example explains how smooth components can encode sharp transitions. Increasing the number of Fourier harmonics narrows the transition region, but also produces the persistent overshoot described by the Gibbs phenomenon. The illustrated square wave and coefficient calculation are mathematical constructions, not measurements of a physical device.

Harmonic power of a square wave (P{r,−r}​/P=8/(π2r2),r odd)

Words: 59
Square wave OurBigBook.com
A zero-mean square wave of amplitude G has total mean-square signal power G2. Each positive odd Fourier harmonic and its negative-frequency partner contribute 8G2/(π2r2), by its exact Fourier coefficients. The fundamental pair therefore accounts for 8/π2 of the total. The sum of contributions above harmonic index R decays on the order of R−1, although the discontinuous waveform still requires arbitrarily high harmonics for exact reconstruction.

Gibbs phenomenon

Words: 296
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
The Gibbs phenomenon is the persistent overshoot near a jump discontinuity in ordinary truncated Fourier series. For this square wave, retain M nonzero odd modes:
QM​(x)=π4​∑k=0M−1​2k+1sin((2k+1)x)​.
(17)
As M grows, the first peak approaches the jump while its height tends to approximately 1.17897974. This is an excess of about 0.17898 above the upper level 1, or 8.949% of the jump size 2. The narrower region does not imply a vanishing maximum error. At the jump itself every QM​(0)=0. These observations are compatible with pointwise convergence and L2 convergence but exclude uniform convergence to the discontinuous square wave. [ref].
For this particular sum, its derivative is QM′​(x)=(2/π)sin(2Mx)/sinx away from multiples of π, so the first positive peak is exactly at x=π/(2M). There,
QM​(2Mπ​)=M2​∑k=0M−1​πuk​sin(πuk​)​,uk​=Mk+1/2​.
(18)
This is a midpoint Riemann sum tending to 2Si(π)/π, where Si is the sine integral. It gives a short explanation of the nonzero limiting excess.
The phenomenon matters whenever a sharp boundary is represented by a limited set of Fourier harmonics: a visible ripple can be a property of the approximation rather than an oscillation in the original profile. Josiah Willard Gibbs reported the phenomenon in his 1899 letter “Fourier's Series” in Nature, volume 59, page 606. This is a documented historical report, without a claim of first discovery. [ref].

Fourier series of a noninteger-frequency sine (sin(λx)∼∑n≥1​π(n2−λ2)2(−1)n+1nsin(πλ)​sin(nx))

Words: 69
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
For real noninteger λ, the periodic extension from [−π,π] has the displayed Fourier series, obtained by the product-to-sum identity in the sine coefficient integral. It equals the original function in the open interval and zero at the periodic endpoint jumps. At λ=1/2, Parseval's identity gives ∑n≥1​n2/(4n2−1)2=π2/64. Integer frequencies instead already belong to the ordinary sine basis and should not be substituted into the removable coefficient singularities without taking limits.

Fourier orthogonality (2π1​∫02π​ei(n−m)tdt=δnm​)

Words: 109
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
The complex exponential functions eint, for integers n, are orthogonal under the normalized integral inner product over a complete period. If n=m, the integrand ei(n−m)t is one; otherwise its antiderivative has equal endpoint values, giving zero. For the real modes, ∫−ππ​cos2(nt)dt=∫−ππ​sin2(nt)dt=π for n≥1, while every mixed sine-cosine integral and every unequal-frequency pairing vanishes.
This makes the coefficient formulas useful: multiply a trigonometric polynomial by one mode and integrate, and all other modes cancel. For f(x)=1/2+cosx+21​sin(2x), integration against cosx gives π, and against sin(2x) gives π/2, recovering a1​=1 and b2​=1/2. Division by the squared norm of the mode supplies the normalization. A full period matters; truncating the integration interval generally destroys these cancellations.

Uniqueness of a trigonometric series outside a finite set

Words: 95
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
If the symmetric partial sums of ∑r∈Z​ar​eirt tend to zero at every point outside a finite set, then all coefficients vanish. Almost-everywhere convergence first gives a±n​→0. The twice-integrated series F(t)=a0​t2/2−∑r=0​ar​eirt/r2 is continuous. Riemann summation of a convergent trigonometric series makes its symmetric second derivative zero away from the exceptional points, so it is affine on each intervening interval. Sinc-squared summation of a sequence tending to zero makes its symmetric first-order quotient zero everywhere, removing all possible affine corners. The globally affine function differs from a periodic function by a0​t2/2, forcing a0​=0; periodicity then makes it constant, and integration against each nonzero frequency gives ar​=0.

Riemann summation of a convergent trigonometric series (∑r​ar​eirtsinc2(rh/2)→∑r​ar​eirt)

Words: 101
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
Suppose the symmetric partial sums converge at a fixed point. Group positive and negative frequencies together, let Sn​ be the resulting partial sums and set w(x)=(sinx/x)2, with w(0)=1. Summation by parts expresses the weighted sum as ∑n≥0​Sn​[w(nk)−w((n+1)k)], where k=∣h∣/2. The total variation of these weights is at most ∫0∞​∣w′(x)∣dx<∞, independently of k, and each fixed difference tends to zero. Subtract the limiting value of Sn​ and split into a finite prefix and a uniformly small tail to prove convergence to that value. This is a regular summation method even though the sinc-squared weights need not decrease monotonically.

Decay of coefficients of an almost-everywhere convergent trigonometric series

Words: 66
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
If symmetric partial sums ∑r=−nn​ar​eirt converge almost everywhere on the circle, then an​,a−n​→0. Their successive differences Tn​=an​eint+a−n​e−int tend to zero almost everywhere. If Mn​=∣an​∣+∣a−n​∣ failed to tend to zero, choose a subsequence with Mn​≥ε. The normalized Tn​/Mn​ are bounded by one and tend to zero almost everywhere, so dominated convergence makes their squared integrals tend to zero. Fourier orthogonality instead makes those integrals (∣an​∣2+∣a−n​∣2)/Mn2​≥1/2, a contradiction.

Periodic triangular bump (bε​(t)=(1−∥t∥/ε)+​)

Words: 71
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
For 0<ε≤1/2, this continuous function on R/Z has nonnegative Fourier coefficients
bε​(r)=ε(πrεsin(πrε)​)2,bε​(0)=ε.
(19)
It is ε−1 times the periodic convolution of two indicators of [−ε/2,ε/2]. Its Fourier series is absolutely convergent, ∑r​bε​(r)=bε​(0)=1, and ∑∣r∣>R​bε​(r)≪1/(εR). Consequently, if all N points tn​ avoid the interval ∥t∥<ε, some frequency 1≤r≪ε−2 satisfies ∣∑n​e(rtn​)∣≫Nε. This detects missing small neighborhoods by a large exponential sum.

Du Bois-Reymond theorem

Words: 34
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
There are continuous functions whose Fourier series diverges at a prescribed point. In contrast, the Fejér kernel is nonnegative and has integral one, so Fejér summation is a uniform-norm contraction. The resulting Fejér sums need not be positive: for the constant function f=−1, every sum is −1.

Smooth-window Fourier coefficients of a periodic distribution (cm​=χf​(2πm))

Words: 43
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
A smooth compactly supported window with ∑j∈Z​χ(x+j)=1 permits multiplying every periodic distribution unambiguously. Its Fourier transform sampled at integer harmonics gives the periodic coefficients. The sharp window H(x)−H(x−1) works for locally integrable functions but can be undefined at singular period endpoints, such as delta derivatives.

In the half-kernel normalization Fn−1​=(2n)−1sin2(nt/2)/sin2(t/2), use Fn−1​(t)≤min{n/2,π2/(2nt2)}. Splitting the convolution error integral at 1/n gives the valid constant Cα​=1/[π(α+1)]+π/(1−α). At the endpoint α=1 this argument instead gives O(Mlogn/n).

Fejér first-moment approximation bound (∥σn​f−f∥∞​≤Cω(f,logn/n))

Words: 122 Articles: 1
Fejér sum OurBigBook.com
The normalized Fejér kernel satisfies 0≤Fn​(t)≤min{n/(2π),π/(2nt2)} on 0<∣t∣≤π. Splitting its first absolute moment at 1/n gives ∫∣t∣Fn​(t)dt≤1/(2πn)+(π/n)log(πn). The chaining inequality for the modulus of continuity, ω(f,t)≤(1+t/δ)ω(f,δ), then bounds the Fejér sum error by ω(f,δ)[1+δ−1∫∣t∣Fn​]. Taking δ=logn/n proves the stated bound for n≥2 and hence uniform convergence for continuous periodic functions. The logarithm vanishes at n=1, so the displayed estimate is not intended at that index.
Fractional-scale Fejér approximation bound (∥σn​f−f∥∞​≤Cα​ω(f,n−α),0<α<1)
Words: 56
Fejér first-moment approximation bound OurBigBook.com
The positive normalized Fejér kernel has a 1/(nt2) tail. Split the error integral at δ=n−α and use the chaining inequality ω(f,t)≤(1+t/δ)ω(f,δ). Its tail contributes at most a constant times nα−1(1+αlogn)ω(f,δ). The factor is uniformly bounded for each fixed α<1, proving the displayed estimate. Its constant need not remain bounded as α tends to one.

Fejér second-modulus approximation bound (∥σn​f−f∥∞​≤(1+π2)ω2​(f,n−1/2))

Words: 95 Articles: 1
Fejér sum OurBigBook.com
The even positive Fejér kernel of total mass one gives σn​f−f=21​∫Fn​(t)[f(⋅+t)−2f+f(⋅−t)]dt. The scaling property of the second modulus of smoothness bounds this by ω2​(f,δ)(1+δ−2∫t2Fn​(t)dt). On [−π,π], sin(∣t∣/2)≥∣t∣/π gives ∫t2Fn​(t)dt≤π2/n. Choose δ=n−1/2. For twice continuously differentiable functions, the second-difference integral formula makes the error O(n−1).
Fejér saturation on a Fourier mode (∥σn​(coskx)−coskx∥∞​=k/n)
Words: 50
Fejér second-modulus approximation bound OurBigBook.com
For fixed positive integer k and n>k, the Fourier coefficient of the Fejér kernel at frequency k multiplies the mode by 1−k/n. The displayed error is exact. Consequently the order n−1 cannot be replaced by o(n−1) for all twice continuously differentiable periodic functions, even though each fixed Fourier mode is infinitely differentiable.

Fejér summation is a uniform-norm contraction (∥σn​f∥∞​≤∥f∥∞​)

Words: 43
Fejér sum OurBigBook.com
The Fejér kernel is nonnegative and has unit mass in its convolution normalization. The integral triangle inequality therefore bounds the supremum norm of a Fejér sum by that of the original function. In the half-kernel convention Fn​=(2n)−1∣∑j=0n−1​eijt∣2, its integral is π and the convolution prefactor is 1/π.

Fourier coefficient (f​n​)

Words: 403 Articles: 7
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
For an integrable function of period L>0, its complex Fourier coefficients measure its inner product with each complex exponential mode:
f​n​=L1​∫x0​x0​+L​f(x)e−2πinx/Ldx.
(30)
For a real function of period 2π, the real coefficient convention of Fourier series gives f​0​=a0​/2 and f​n​=(an​−ibn​)/2 for n≥1, with f​−n​=f​n​​. For f(x)=1/2+cosx+21​sin(2x), the only nonzero complex Fourier coefficients are f​0​=1/2, f​±1​=1/2, f​2​=−i/4, and f​−2​=i/4. This explains why the real and complex lists look different while representing the same function.

Fourier coefficient decay (∣an​∣+∣bn​∣=O(n−p))

Words: 42
Fourier coefficient OurBigBook.com
The rate at which Fourier coefficients approach zero as their index increases. The differentiability of the periodic extension, including matching values and derivatives at its joins, controls this rate through integration by parts. An absolutely bounded tail O(n−p) with p>1 gives a uniform truncation error O(N1−p).

Fourier sine coefficient (bn​=L1​∫−LL​f(x)sin(nπx/L)dx)

Words: 60
Fourier coefficient OurBigBook.com
For an integrable function on [−L,L], with L>0 and integer n≥1, the displayed Fourier coefficient multiplies the mode sin(nπx/L) in its real Fourier series. Fourier orthogonality fixes the normalization because the squared mode has integral L. If f is odd, the product with the sine is even, so bn​=(2/L)∫0L​f(x)sin(nπx/L)dx. These are also the coefficients of the Fourier sine series of the restriction to (0,L).

Periodic dilation annihilates low Fourier modes (∫T​f(nx)eimxdx=0(0<∣m∣<n))

Words: 67
Fourier coefficient OurBigBook.com
If f is integrable and 2π-periodic and n is a positive integer, then ∫02π​f(nx)eimxdx=0 for every integer m with 0<∣m∣<n. Split the integral into n equal intervals and substitute y=nx−2πj to obtain
n1​∫02π​f(y)eimy/ndy∑j=0n−1​e2πimj/n=0.
(31)
The root of unity sum vanishes by the finite geometric series formula. The zero mode is ∫f, so a mean-zero dilated function is orthogonal to all trigonometric polynomials of degree at most n−1.

Absolute Fourier convergence from a square-integrable derivative (∑n=0​∣f​(n)∣≤(π/3​)∥f′∥2​)

Words: 47
Fourier coefficient OurBigBook.com
For a periodic absolutely continuous function with derivative in L2, integration by parts gives f′​(n)=inf​(n). Bessel's inequality and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality prove the displayed bound in the normalized circle norm. Adding the constant coefficient gives an absolutely and uniformly convergent Fourier series. Merely bounding individual coefficients by O(1/∣n∣) would not establish absolute convergence.

Uniqueness of Fourier coefficients in L1

Words: 41
Fourier coefficient OurBigBook.com
If a periodic integrable function has all Fourier coefficients zero, it vanishes almost everywhere. Its Fejér sums vanish, whereas the Fejér kernel is an approximate identity and converges to that function in the integrable norm. Applied to a periodized squared Fourier transform, this detects orthogonality of integer translates.

Fourier coefficient decay of an analytic periodic function

Words: 41
Fourier coefficient OurBigBook.com
If a periodic function extends analytically and remains bounded in a nonzero complex strip around the real axis, contour shifting gives constants C,c>0 such that
∣f​n​∣≤Ce−c∣n∣.
(32)
This exponential decay underlies spectral convergence of Fourier approximation and periodic trapezoidal quadrature.

Termwise differentiation of a Fourier series

Words: 26
Fourier coefficient OurBigBook.com
When regularity and convergence justify termwise differentiation, the derivative of a Fourier mode multiplies its coefficient by its frequency. For period L,
f′​n​=L2πin​f​n​.
(33)

Fourier cosine series

Words: 358 Articles: 6
Fourier series OurBigBook.com
A Fourier cosine series has the form
2a0​​+∑n=1∞​an​cos(nx).
(34)
It represents the even function obtained by reflecting its data across the origin.

Half-integer cosine expansion of a linear profile (L−x=π28L​∑n≥0​(2n+1)2cos((2n+1)πx/(2L))​)

Words: 87
Fourier cosine series OurBigBook.com
For L>0 and 0≤x≤L, set μn​=(2n+1)π/(2L). The cosine modes satisfy a homogeneous Neumann boundary condition at zero and a homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition at L. Their squared norm is L/2, and integration by parts gives
∫0L​(L−x)cos(μn​x)dx=μn2​1−cos(μn​L)​=μn2​1​.
(35)
Thus their Fourier coefficients are 2/(Lμn2​), proving the displayed formula by Sturm-Liouville theory. One can also obtain completeness by extending evenly across zero and oddly across L: the resulting continuous 4L-periodic extension has only odd-index cosine modes. The n−2 coefficient bound proves uniform convergence, including both endpoints. This expansion supplies the initial transient for a heat equation with mixed endpoint conditions.

Even extension (Fe​(x)=f(∣x∣))

Words: 28
Fourier cosine series OurBigBook.com
The even extension of a function f:[0,L]→R is Fe​(x)=f(∣x∣) for −L≤x≤L. It is an even function. Its 2L-periodic extension is the function expanded by the half-range Fourier cosine series.

Quadratic arch expansion in half-integer cosine modes (b2−y2=π332b2​∑n≥0​(2n+1)3(−1)ncos((2n+1)πy/(2b))​)

Words: 75
Fourier cosine series OurBigBook.com
For b>0 and −b≤y≤b, the even quadratic polynomial b2−y2 has the displayed expansion in even Dirichlet eigenfunctions. Put kn​=(2n+1)π/(2b). Their squared norm on [−b,b] is b. Two integrations by parts, using cos(kn​b)=0, give
∫−bb​(b2−y2)cos(kn​y)dy=kn​2​∫−bb​ysin(kn​y)dy=kn3​4sin(kn​b)​.
(36)
Division by b gives the displayed Fourier coefficients. The cubic decay gives uniform convergence. The half-integer frequencies arise from requiring both evenness and zero values at the endpoints, rather than from a periodic boundary condition. This expansion is useful in rectangular duct flow.

Fourier cosine coefficient (an​=L2​∫0L​f(x)cos(nπx/L)dx)

Words: 33
Fourier cosine series OurBigBook.com
On [0,L], the Fourier cosine series convention f(x)=a0​/2+∑n≥1​an​cos(nπx/L) uses the displayed coefficients, including n=0. Orthogonality of the cosine modes gives these formulas for square-integrable functions; the expansion is interpreted in the L2 norm until stronger convergence is established.

Half-range Fourier cosine series (f(x)=a0​/2+∑n≥1​an​cos(nπx/L))

Words: 116 Articles: 1
Fourier cosine series OurBigBook.com
For a function prescribed on 0<x<L, its half-range Fourier cosine series is the Fourier series of the even extension, made 2L-periodic. Its coefficients are an​=(2/L)∫0L​f(x)cos(nπx/L)dx, including n=0. At a jump the usual piecewise-smooth convergence theorem gives the average of the two one-sided limits of the periodic extension.

Fourier cosine coefficients of a sine mode (an​=4m/[π(m2−n2)] when m,n have opposite parity)

Words: 68
Half-range Fourier cosine series OurBigBook.com
For a positive integer m, take f(x)=sin(mx) on 0<x<π and form its half-range Fourier cosine series. The product-to-sum identity gives
an​=π1​[m+n1−(−1)m+n​+m−n1−(−1)m−n​],n≥0, n=m.
(37)
Thus an​=4m/[π(m2−n2)] for opposite parity and zero for the same parity. The exceptional integral am​=(2/π)∫0π​sin(mx)cos(mx)dx is zero. The constant term is a0​/2, not a0​. These coefficients represent the even periodic extension, not the original sine wave on negative arguments. Their quadratic decay gives absolute convergence.

x3−π2x=12∑n=1∞​n3(−1)n​sin(nx).
